subject: Anuran roadside calling survey-- how to deal with ordinal outcome?

messages.author: 7546378a8e4b0f4b
messages.subject: Anuran roadside calling survey-- how to deal with ordinal outcome?
parts:
Dear unmarked users,

I am new to this field. 

I conducted anuran roadside calling survey in Taiwan by adapting the method from the North American Amphibian Monitoring Program (NAAMP).

The calling index (i.e. 0-3) was used  to represent the relative abundance of a specific anuran.

I would like to use "unmarked" package taking into accounts detection probability to assess the association between land use variables and anuran relative abundance. 

Previous studies generally converted the calling index into a binary variable (i.e. presence/absence; 1/0); however, I think this measure may lead to loss of information. 

In my study area, an anuran species had 100% occupancy rate. This species indeed significantly and positively associated with the area of agricultural land according to multivariate linear regression. 

However, When I converted  the calling index to binary outcome and assessed the relationships between land use variables and this species by occupancy model (occu function) or multi-season occupancy model (colext), none of land use variables were associated with the occurrence. This is may due to the 100% occupancy rate of this species.

I am currently trying to use the N-mixture model (pcount function in unmarked) in this case and input the original values of calling index into the model. But I am not sure is it appropriate to use pcount function for calling index, a ordinal data? Or should I use the other functions?

Could unmarked package deal with the ordinal data?

I would greatly appreciate it if you could give me any suggestions. Thank you very much.

Chau-Ren

messages.author: 5fb191f8527859e2
messages.subject: Aw: [unmarked] Anuran roadside calling survey-- how to deal with ordinal outcome?
parts:
I think you should try to use the unmarked function occuMS() with the multinomial parameterization. I think this would be more appropriate for your data than pcount().

Best wishes,

Beni
